analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act and claws back its unspent money.
analysis.headline: The repeal bill, introduced by one Republican with 24 cosponsors, was sent to eight House committees and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-sentence bill would erase the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 in its entirety and take back every dollar from that law that had not yet been spent. That law includes Medicare's new power to negotiate drug prices, a $35 monthly insulin cap and a $2,000 out-of-pocket cap for seniors, extended help with health insurance premiums, the largest clean energy tax-credit program in U.S. history, a 15% minimum tax on very large corporations, a tax on stock buybacks, and fees on oil and gas companies' excess methane leaks. Repealing it would end all of that at once, restoring lower taxes for large corporations and freeing drug makers, oil producers, and polluters from the fees and price limits the law imposed.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug makers would regain the revenue they gave up under Medicare price negotiation; oil and gas companies would be freed from the methane emissions charge and increased leasing fees; large corporations would escape the 15% corporate minimum tax and the 1% excise tax on stock buybacks; and very high-income households that profit from those provisions would keep more of their gains. Investors in those companies would also benefit if repeal lifted the expected hit to their earnings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drug makers, oil companies, and large corporations

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Public Law 117-169 (the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022) in its entirety, ending every program, tax, and fee created by that law.
It also rescinds all unobligated funds from the 2022 law, meaning money Congress had appropriated but not yet spent — including clean energy and climate investments — would be taken back.

Repeal would restore the pre-2022 status quo for Medicare drug pricing, meaning drug makers would no longer face negotiated lower prices, the $35 insulin cap, or the $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap for seniors.

Repeal would eliminate the law's 15% corporate minimum tax on companies with over $1 billion in profits and the excise tax on stock buybacks, and would end the charge on oil and gas companies' methane emissions.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries would lose the drug price negotiation results, the $35 insulin cap, and the $2,000 out-of-pocket cap, and would pay more for prescriptions. The roughly millions of people who buy coverage through the Affordable Care Act marketplaces would face higher premiums when the extended premium subsidies disappear. Households and businesses would lose clean energy tax credits for solar, electric vehicles, and home efficiency, and communities hosting those investments would lose the promised spending. Taxpayers would lose the deficit reduction the 2022 law was scored to produce.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare patients, ACA enrollees, and energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The strongest argument for repeal was fiscal: supporters of the 2022 law's opponents argued its roughly $700 billion in new spending and energy regulation contributed to inflation and that rescinding unspent funds would reduce the deficit. repeal would remove those commitments but also remove the offsetting taxes and fees, likely increasing deficits over ten years according to independent budget analysts.

Repeal would claw back tax credits that companies and households had already counted on when making long-term investments in solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles, creating sudden losses for projects underway at the time of repeal.
Seniors currently relying on the insulin cap, the out-of-pocket cap, and negotiated drug prices would lose those protections immediately upon enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow to drug companies, oil producers, and large corporations; the costs fall on Medicare beneficiaries, marketplace enrollees, and households counting on clean energy credits. The fiscal argument for repeal is weaker than it appears because the 2022 law's spending was paired with taxes and fees that repeal would also eliminate. As drafted, the bill offers nothing for ordinary people in exchange for removing their protections.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to eight separate House committees on the day it was introduced, none of which took it up, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Andrew Ogles introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined by 20 original cosponsors, all Republicans.

The Speaker referred it to eight committees at once — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Agriculture, Natural Resources, Financial Services, Science, Space and Technology, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Oversight — a referral pattern that divides jurisdiction so broadly that no single committee must act on it.
The only subsequent action was a referral to the Transportation Subcommittee on Highways and Transit on February 3, 2023; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The bill ended the 118th Congress with 24 cosponsors and no floor action, so the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 remained in force with its programs, taxes, and fees intact.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries, Affordable Care Act enrollees, and clean energy industries kept the law's protections and credits because the repeal never advanced; drug makers, oil and gas companies, and large corporations did not get the tax relief and fee removal they would have gained from repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Seniors and clean energy firms kept IRA benefits

for.name: Rep. Andrew Ogles
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 and rescind its unspent funds.

for.name: 24 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill; no Democrat joined.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to eight committees simultaneously and never scheduled it for a floor vote despite a Republican majority, so it never advanced past referral.

against.name: House committees of referral
against.role: Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Agriculture, Natural Resources, Financial Services, Science, Space and Technology, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Oversight
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in February 2023 and scheduled no hearing or markup on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the repeal, and the bill never reached a vote in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: Repeal would end the methane emissions charge and higher leasing and royalty fees the 2022 law imposed on their operations, while leaving the public to absorb the pollution and the lost revenue. Their gain comes directly from removing a cost the law placed on their emissions.

Repeal would end Medicare's price negotiation, the $35 insulin cap, and the $2,000 out-of-pocket cap, restoring revenue the industry gave up under the 2022 law. Their gain means seniors pay more for the same drugs.

Repeal would eliminate the 15% minimum tax on billion-dollar-profit corporations and the excise tax on stock buybacks, two of the main offsets that made the 2022 law deficit-neutral. The benefit flows to the most profitable firms and their shareholders.

industries.industry: Clean energy and electric vehicle industries
industries.note: Repeal and the rescission of unobligated funds would erase the tax credits and grants that the solar, wind, battery, and EV supply chain industries were built on, killing projects mid-stream. Their interest in defeating the bill ran alongside consumers' interest in cheaper clean energy.

Repeal would end the extended ACA premium subsidies that keep millions of subsidized customers in marketplace plans, shrinking insurer enrollment. Insurers' interest in keeping the subsidies coincided with enrollees' interest in affordable premiums.
